title: Slow-cooker French onion soup
subtitle: Deeply sweet, caramelised onions in a rich beef broth
excerpt: Onions caramelised over several hours in the slow cooker, then finished with wine and beef stock. Serve with cheese toasts floating on top for the full effect.
sourceNotes: Soupe à l'oignon gratinée is a classic of French bistro cooking, documented by Auguste Escoffier in Le Guide Culinaire (1903) and later by Julia Child in Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961). The slow-cooker method caramelises onions without supervision.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the soup base before adding the cheese toasts. Reheat and add toasts fresh when serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup base keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days. Reheat and add toasts when ready to serve.
recipe.temperatureNote: Grill temperature for toasting the cheese

content.text: The secret to French onion soup is time. The onions must become deeply sweet and golden; anything less and the soup will taste sharp and raw. The slow cooker does this extremely well. Set it on HIGH with the lid cracked open slightly, and the onions will caramelise over 5 to 6 hours without any stirring or risk of burning.
This recipe has two stages: caramelising the onions, then adding wine and stock to make the soup. Both happen in the same pot.
Serve in deep oven-safe bowls with a slice of toasted bread topped with melted cheese floating on top.

Add {{onion}} of thinly sliced onions to the slow cooker with {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and {{caster-sugar}} of sugar. Stir well. Set the slow cooker to HIGH and prop the lid open slightly with a wooden spoon. Cook for 5 to 6 hours, stirring once or twice. The onions are ready when they are deep golden brown and very soft.

Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} of dry white wine and stir it through the onions. Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, {{thyme}} of thyme, and {{bay-leaves}} of bay. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt. Set to LOW and cook for a further 1 hour. Discard the thyme and bay.

Set your grill to high. Place {{bread}} of toasted bread slices on a baking tray. Pile {{cheddar}} of grated cheese onto each slice. Grill for 2 to 3 minutes until the cheese is melted and bubbling. Ladle the soup into bowls and float a cheese toast on top.

rows.symptom: The onions are not caramelising after 5 hours
rows.cause: The lid was fully on, which trapped steam and kept the onions wet rather than browning them.
rows.fix: Cook uncovered on HIGH for a further hour. The water needs to evaporate before browning can happen. Prop the lid next time.

rows.cause: The onions caramelised very fully and the sugar added extra sweetness.
rows.fix: Add a splash of balsamic vinegar or red wine vinegar to balance. Taste after each addition.

rows.symptom: The broth tastes thin and pale
rows.cause: The stock was too weak, or too much water diluted it.
rows.fix: Simmer uncovered on HIGH for 20 minutes to reduce and concentrate. Or add a stock cube dissolved in a little hot water.

rows.symptom: The cheese toast has sunk into the soup
rows.cause: The toast was too thin or too soft when placed on top.
rows.fix: Use a thick slice of bread and toast it well before adding cheese. Serve the soup very hot so the toast floats rather than sinking.

content.text: French onion soup is one of the great bistro dishes of Paris, where it was served in the early hours as a restorative to workers and night owls at Les Halles market. The combination of deeply sweet onions, wine, beef broth, and melted cheese is one of the most satisfying things a kitchen can produce. The slow cooker handles the hardest part: getting the onions dark enough without burning them.
